name: Apelles
title: Faithful Christian in Rome, Proven in Christ
summary: In his greeting list to the church in Rome, Paul mentions Apelles with a special honorific: 'the one who has stood the test in Christ' (Greek: dokimos). This expression indicates a believer who has undergone trials and proven genuine in faith, just as metal is tested by fire. Apelles is one of over 26 named individuals in Romans chapter 16, a unique greeting list that offers a rare glimpse into the diversity and social breadth of the early Christian community in Rome. Beyond this brief but telling mention, we know nothing more about Apelles from the New Testament.

footnotes.text: The name Apelles (Greek: Ἀπελλῆς) is of Greco-Roman origin and was a common name in the Hellenistic world. It is also known from the famous Greek painter Apelles of Cos (4th century BC). The name was widespread among both free citizens and freed slaves in the Roman Empire.

Romans chapter 16 contains a remarkably long list of greetings with over 26 named individuals. This list provides valuable insight into the early Christian church in Rome, which consisted of a diverse group with various ethnic and social backgrounds—including Jews, Gentiles, slaves, freedmen, and Roman citizens.

The expression 'the one who has stood the test in Christ' (Greek: τὸν δόκιμον ἐν Χριστῷ) uses the word 'dokimos,' meaning 'tested and found genuine,' just as metal is tested by fire. This was a strongly affirming expression indicating that Apelles had undergone trials and proven himself faithful in the faith.

Some early church fathers, including Origen, have speculated whether Apelles may have been one of the seventy disciples whom Jesus sent out (Luke 10:1), but there is no certain historical documentation for this. In the Byzantine tradition, he is counted among the seventy apostles and said to have become bishop in Smyrna or Herakleia.
